items.title: v) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Reactions (ΔHr) using Bond Energies

source_refs.note: v) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Reactions (ΔHr) using Bond Energies: a main subheading of 6.8 Hess's law of heat summation, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 128-130.

blocks.text: A special case of Hess’ law involves the use of bond energies to estimate heats of reaction for gas-phase reactions. In the first step, the bonds in all the reactant molecules are broken to give free atoms in the gas phase. The enthalpy change for this step can be calculated by adding the bond enthalpies from Table 6.1. In the second step, the product molecules are formed. The enthalpy change for this step can again be estimated from the bond enthalpies of Table 6.1, which must now be taken with minus sign because the bonds are being formed instead of broken. In general, the heat of reaction for any gaseous chemical reaction can be calculated from average B.E.’s by use of the following version of Hess’ law:

blocks.alt: Triangle: 'Reactants' arrow to 'Products' labelled delta H(o)rxn in red; 'Reactants' arrow down to 'Atoms' labelled E(R); 'Atoms' arrow up to 'Products' labelled E(P).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: Hess Cycle; showing the relationship between B.E.’s and ΔHr. = ∑n ER – ∑n EP (original drawing after the textbook's second Figure 6.4).

blocks.text: Sample problem 6.7 In the case of formation of HCl(g) from H₂(g) and Cl₂(g), use B.E. data from Table 6.1 to estimate ΔH for the reaction:
And finally calculate the heat of formation of HCl.
We replace this reaction by a hypothetical two-step process. The bonds in all the reactant molecules are first broken, and then the atoms are combined to make the products.
EH–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹ ; ECl–Cl = 242 kJ mol⁻¹
The standard enthalpy change in the reaction is obtained by the following formula:
Enthalpy of formation of HCl, = –184/2 kJ = –92 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 436 kJ + 242 kJ = 678 kJ, not 478 kJ; the book’s diagram and the next step (678 – 862 = –184 kJ) use 678 kJ.

blocks.alt: Hess triangle for Sample Problem 6.7. H2(g) + Cl2(g) on the left is joined to 2HCl(g) on the right by a straight arrow labelled delta Hr degree (the direct route). Below, a curved arrow goes from H2(g) + Cl2(g) down to 2H(g) + 2Cl(g), and a second curved arrow goes from 2H(g) + 2Cl(g) up to 2HCl(g) (the route through the atoms).
blocks.caption: Hess triangle for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g): the direct route (ΔHr°) and the route through the atoms 2H(g) + 2Cl(g) (printed beside the ΔHr° lines, no caption in the book).

blocks.text: The energy cycle is shown below:

blocks.alt: Energy-level diagram. Top level: 2 H & 2 Cl atoms (two blue and two red balls). Middle level on the left: H2 & Cl2 molecules (blue H-H and red Cl-Cl). Lowest level on the right: 2 HCl molecules. A grey arrow up from the middle to the top level: delta HR = +678 kJ. A grey arrow down from the top to the lowest level: delta HP = -862 kJ. A thick black arrow down from the middle to the lowest level: delta Hrxn = -184 kJ.
blocks.caption: Hess’ Cycle; showing the relationship between B.E.’s and ΔH. (original drawing after the figure printed with Sample Problem 6.7, p129 of the textbook).

blocks.prompt:
a) The reaction for the Haber process is:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
The relevant bond energies are:
EN≡N = 945 kJ mol⁻¹, EH–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹, EN–H = 391 kJ mol⁻¹.
Calculate the enthalpy change of the above reaction.
blocks.explanation: Bonds broken: 1 N≡N + 3 H–H = 945 + 3 × 436 = 2253 kJ. Bonds formed: 6 N–H in 2NH₃ = 6 × 391 = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ (for 2 mol of NH₃).

blocks.prompt:
b) Calculate the enthalpy change for the following reaction
C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)
The bond energies of various bonds (in kJ mol⁻¹) are given below:
EC–C = +347, EC–H = +410, EC–O = +336, EO=O = +496, EC=O = +805, EO–H = +465
blocks.explanation: Bonds broken: in ethanol 1 C–C (347) + 5 C–H (2050) + 1 C–O (336) + 1 O–H (465), and 3 O=O (1488); total 4686 kJ. Bonds formed: 4 C=O in 2CO₂ (3220) and 6 O–H in 3H₂O (2790); total 6010 kJ. ΔH = 4686 − 6010 = −1324 kJ mol⁻¹ (bond energies are for gases, so this is only an estimate).
